Morning all

Nichola

 
 




Trial week 2 – w/c 20 October 2025
Week two of the PDD Trial focused on the issue of what are conditions which are “reasonably likely to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use” for the
 purposes of identifying prohibited defeat devices in the Defendants’ vehicles.
The evidence on this issue includes:

Expert evidence on normal driving conditions prepared by Professor Hausberger for the Mercedes Defendants and Dr Tate for the Claimants (this evidence considered
 data and statistics on the range of typical driving, how fast people drive, how hard they accelerate etc); andExpert evidence on climatology prepared by Professor Chapman for the VW Defendants and Professor Mills for the ClaimantsAdditionally, Vauxhall rely on work by Professor Pope in respect of climatology but he has not been engaged as an expert in these proceedings.
 
Mr Adam Kramer KC introduced Dr Tate and his evidence and Mr Malcolm Sheehan KC conducted a cross-examination of Dr Tate for the Mercedes Defendants. Mr Sheehan KC’s cross-examination
 focused on a number of corrections Dr Tate had made to his report including clarifying his evidence on how long comparable vehicles spend in the operating windows of conditions which would trigger defeat devices in normal vehicle operation and use. Dr Tate
 had initially presented these figures as percentages of the periods of acceleration where emissions control systems would be de-rated given that emissions are mostly produced during periods of acceleration. Subsequently Dr Tate provided additional detail in
 respect of the periods of time during whole trips and the periods when the vehicle is moving. Mr Sheehan KC also questioned Dr Tate on whether there were errors in his calculations and attacked the comparability of the vehicles Dr Tate had with the sample
 vehicles in the Mercedes proceedings, suggesting that he had overplayed the operation window of certain defeat devices as a result.
 
Mr Sheehan KC introduced Professor Hausberger and his evidence and Mr Kramer KC conducted a cross-examination of Professor Hausberger for the Claimants. Mr Kramer KC’s cross-examination
 focused on the significant funding which Professor Hausberger has received from the car manufacturer industry for research during his career and the objectively ridiculous conclusions he had set out in his report. For example, Professor Hausberger’s report
 stated that the maximum speed which could be considered normal is 101km/h (although a higher speed could be used in a journey without it being abnormal, but only if it was less than 5% of the time), this is below the speed limit on many roads. In addition
 to this, Professor Hausberger had stated that the maximum length of a normal journey is 46 minutes.  Professor Hausberger was inflexible on these limits under some good cross-examination which undermined his evidence somewhat
 
The climatology evidence was less contentious as the experts agreed that each other’s methods were sound and provide different statistical views on the conditions likely
 to be encountered. Professor Chapman (for the Defendants) provided a series of average temperatures for the UK and all the countries in the EU as well as smaller regions for different months and seasons, he also weighted these averages according to population.
 Professor Mills (for the Claimants) provided detail regarding the full range of temperatures experienced across the EU and the number of people who experience such temperatures and for how long in a given year.  Both these experts provided information about
 altitudes which are encountered in the EU and the UK. Lady Justice Cockerill was grateful for their evidence and noted that this was unlikely to be a significant part of the judgment but that it was invaluable to have this information and the limitations of
 the different approaches available to her for consideration.
 
We think that the Claimants’ evidence and cross-examination of the Defendants’ experts has clearly had a positive impact on the judge’s views of this element of the case.
 While we anticipate that the likely approach Lady Justice Cockerill will take is to set a limit on the range of conditions which would reasonably be encountered during normal vehicle operation and use, however, we do not expect that she will be inclined to
 adopt an excessively restrictive set of boundaries (which the Defendants have advocated for) in light of the Claimants’ case on this issue.

Subject: Re: Public access to documents/ Draft letter to Defendants
 






Adam, Gareth, Anna,




With apologies for chasing, the draft letter will resolve a few issues that have arisen in correspondence recently:





Mishcon (for the third parties) wrote to the parties asking for correspondence on the third party folder, and the transcripts.

We wrote to the Defendants saying (i) we will shortly provide the correspondence (and attached the attached clip), (ii) do you agree that we can share transcripts?

HSKF replied that they were considering our email.

We shared the correspondence with Mishcon, but not the transcripts, noting that we were awaiting the Defendants' position on them.





The Defendants have now criticised us for sharing the correspondence with the third parties, in the attached email chain.  My views on their criticisms are:





If the Defendants were concerned about third parties seeing the correspondence, they would have written to the third parties asking them to delete it.  Instead they have removed them from
 the chain.  (i.e. where are the red exclamation mark emails to Mishcon telling them to delete confidential information from their inboxes?)

The Defendants have misunderstood our email.  We said (i) we will share documents shortly, and (ii) do you consent to providing transcripts.  We note that you have not replied to (ii); please
 do so.

Under the DDH order, the parts of amber documents that are referred to turn green.  (DDH judgment paras 9, 76, 77: "the very deployment of an Amber document will have the effect of turning
 it from Amber to Green".)

The only sections of amber documents referred to in the clip, which are laughably tiny and largely unintelligible (see, e.g., p.40 of the clip), are those parts that the Defendants themselves
 agree have been referred to by the Claimants, i.e., have turned green, and so third parties are entitled to see.

The Defendants are attempting to collateral use of the Claimants with collateral use of third parties.  We refer to our attached letter [our letter deals with this in more detail].

There is no principled basis on which the Defendants could have objected to us sharing the correspondence with third parties, and we note that no Defendant has in fact provided one (beyond
 their misunderstanding of the DDH order and their attempt to impose our collateral use restrictions on third parties).

We copy the third parties to this email, as the Defendants are attempting to amend via correspondence an order granted following their submissions.  We repeat that if the Defendants seek to
 amend the DDH Order they should do so by an application on notice to third parties.

We are happy for this issue to be raised with the Court and suggest housekeeping next week.








Matt
































​​​​




























Matt Hunt









(He/Him)
